messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh was 58, a product manager at a mid-sized tech firm, married for thirty years, and he had not spoken about the torture in twenty-five. In his home country, he had been a student organizer, and one night military police dragged him from his apartment. They hooded him, spun him until he lost his bearings, and throughout the hours that followed, voices spoke a language he could almost understand but never quite grasp—sharp, overlapping, incomprehensible chatter that circled him while he was blindfolded. Sirens wailed outside the building for what felt like hours, part of the disorientation. They did not need to do much else physically; the dizziness, the confusion, the alternation between silence and sound was enough to break something in him. He managed to leave the country, eventually settled in the United States, found work, married, had children—but the past had come with him.

Now, in the open-plan office where colleagues chattered in different accents and languages over coffee, Rajesh found his chest tightening. He did not know why; he only knew that certain sounds—a burst of laughter in a language he didn't recognize, the high-pitched shriek of a nearby ambulance siren—sent a jolt through him that lingered for hours. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that there was something about him, some intrinsic fault, that had made the torture happen. He was certain that nothing good could come to him anymore; his life was already used up. These beliefs drove him to avoid anything that could be stressful. He took the least visible projects at work, refused to attend team retreats, and left the room if anyone raised their voice. He also began to monitor his body constantly: checking his pulse, scanning for any sign of dizziness or physical oddness, because if he could catch danger early, maybe he could prevent it. But the monitoring itself made him notice every fleeting sensation, and a slight wobble on his feet would instantly pull him back to the spinning hood.

Because he believed he was fundamentally flawed and that others were not to be trusted, Rajesh could not relax even when he knew he was safe. At home, he woke several times a night to check the locks and listen for sirens. He reacted with a full-body startle when his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly. This constant vigilance fed his avoidance: he was so jumpy that he stopped going to crowded grocery stores, and he asked his wife to drive past the police station on a different route. His startle to touch meant he recoiled from handshakes and avoided physical proximity with colleagues. He was certain that any moment of relaxation would invite disaster.

The threat state also made him hypersensitive to triggers. Because he was already on high alert, a distant siren would grab his attention before anyone else noticed. A low murmur of voices from the next cubicle—incomprehensible chatter—would make his mouth go dry and his head spin. Dizziness, which had been a tool of his torturers, now emerged whenever he stood quickly, but because he was watching for it, he magnified it into a full-blown trigger. His avoidance, in turn, strengthened his negative appraisals. By never letting himself near uniforms or sirens, he never tested whether he could survive them. He avoided social situations where conflict might arise, which only confirmed that people were untrustworthy. And each time he monitored his body and caught a hint of dizziness, he saw it as proof that there was still something wrong with him, that the torture had broken him permanently.

The cycle tightened over months. At work, he declined a promotion that would have required more visibility. His wife complained that he never went out with her anymore, that he checked the doors three times before bed, that he flinched every time she touched him. Rajesh knew this was not normal, but he was convinced that nothing good could happen, so what was the point? It was only after a company-wide fire drill—sirens blaring, people shouting incomprehensibly—that he collapsed in the stairwell, unable to breathe. His manager told him to take leave. Now he sits in a therapist’s office, not sure what he hopes for, but certain that he cannot keep living this way. What frightens him most is the possibility that he is right: that nothing can change, and that the fault is still inside him. But he came anyway.
